**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, sitting at the kitchen table with a math worksheet smeared with eraser dust. The numbers blurred together, and my fingers ached from gripping the pencil too tight. His voice wasn’t loud—it didn’t need to be. The words settled in my chest like a stone dropped into a well, and I’ve been carrying them ever since.

Words are strange that way. They don’t occupy space, not like a chair or a book or a body, but they *take up room*. They press against your ribs, hum in your ears at 3 a.m., wrap around your ankles when you’re trying to run. Some words are feathers—*"I love you,"* whispered in the dark, *"You can do this,"* scribbled on a napkin. Others are anvils. *"You’ll never be enough."* *"Why can’t you just be normal?"* *"I don’t know you anymore."*

I’ve spent years trying to measure them. If a compliment is a gram, how many kilograms is a betrayal? If a joke is a breath of air, how much does a secret weigh when it’s finally spoken?

---

II.

There’s a café near my apartment where the barista remembers my order. *"Usual?"* she asks, already reaching for the oat milk. Her name is Lila, and she has a tattoo of a fox on her wrist. *"Vulpes vulpes,"* she told me once, when I asked. *"Just because something’s common doesn’t mean it’s not wild."*

I go there to write, or at least, to pretend to write. Mostly, I stare at the screen and think about the way my mother’s hands shook when she signed the divorce papers. The pen made a sound like a nail scratching glass. My father didn’t look at her. He just stood up, straightened his tie, and said, *"This is for the best."* Three words. A lifetime of silence after.

Lila slides my coffee across the counter. *"You look like you’re thinking too hard,"* she says. I laugh, but it comes out wrong—more like a cough. *"Just counting,"* I tell her.

*"Counting what?"*

*"Words. The ones that matter. The ones that don’t."*

She studies me for a second, then nods like this makes sense. *"You know,"* she says, *"the Inuit have fifty words for snow. But ‘snow’ in English covers all of it—powder, slush, the kind that sticks to your boots. Maybe we’re just bad at naming things."*

I want to ask her if she thinks some things are unnameable. If there’s a word for the way your stomach twists when you realize you’ve become the person you swore you’d never be. But the café is busy, and she’s already turned to the next customer.

---

III.

I had a professor in college who believed language was a cage. *"We think we’re free,"* he’d say, pacing the front of the lecture hall, *"but we’re just rearranging the same twenty-six bars."* He’d write *SATIRE* on the board in all caps, then cross it out. *"Even rebellion has a script."*

One day, I stayed after class to ask him about poetry. *"Isn’t that the point?"* I said. *"To escape the cage?"*

He leaned back in his chair, steepling his fingers. *"Poetry isn’t escape,"* he said. *"It’s the locksmith’s manual. You learn how the cage is built so you can pick the damn thing open. But you’re still inside."*

I didn’t understand then. I do now.

The cage isn’t the words. It’s the space between them. The things we don’t say. The letters we delete. The texts we draft and never send. My father and I haven’t spoken in three years. I have a draft in my emails titled *"Re:"* with no subject, no body, just a cursor blinking like a slow heartbeat.

What do you say to someone who taught you that love was conditional? How do you weigh the silence between *"I’m sorry"* and *"It’s too late"*?

---

IV.

Last winter, I found a bird on my windowsill. A sparrow, small and still, its feathers ruffled against the cold. I cupped my hands around it, felt the rapid flutter of its heart. For a second, I thought it was dead. Then it blinked.

I don’t know why I remember this now. Maybe because holding something fragile makes you realize how heavy your own hands are.

I took the bird inside, wrapped it in a towel, Googled *"how to save a dying sparrow."* The internet said: *Keep it warm. Keep it quiet. Don’t force it to eat.* So I sat on the couch with the bundle in my lap and waited.

It died anyway.

I buried it in the park under an oak tree, using my hands to dig through the frozen earth. My fingers went numb. When I got home, I washed them under scalding water and cried, not because of the bird, but because I couldn’t stop thinking about my mother’s hands. How they used to braid my hair. How they trembled when she signed those papers.

Grief is just love with nowhere to go.

---

V.

Lila is closing up the café when I come in tonight. The lights are dim, and the espresso machine hisses like a sleeping dragon. *"You’re here late,"* she says.

*"Couldn’t sleep."*

She doesn’t ask why. Instead, she makes me a chamomile tea and slides it across the counter. *"My grandma used to say tea fixes everything,"* she tells me. *"She was full of shit, but the ritual helps."*

I wrap my hands around the cup. The heat seeps into my palms. *"What’s your word for this?"* I ask. *"The quiet when everything’s closed and the world feels smaller?"*

She thinks for a minute. *"‘Liminal,’"* she says. *"But that’s not quite it. Maybe there isn’t one."*

*"Maybe we need to make one up."*

*"Maybe."* She wipes down the counter, the cloth making slow, deliberate circles. *"Or maybe some things don’t need names. Maybe they’re just… felt."*

I take a sip of tea. It’s too hot, but I swallow anyway.

---

VI.

I’ve used 997 words. Three left.

Here’s what I know:

1. Words are heavy.
2. Silence is heavier.
3. Some cages don’t have doors.

(But sometimes, if you’re lucky, you find a window.)
